Producers to primary consumers: 42/500 = 0.084, so 8.4%. Primary to secondary: 4.2/42 = 0.10, so 10%. Ecological efficiency is hardly ever above 10% because most of the energy that comes into a trophic level never ends up as new body mass at the next one. Three ways it's lost: (1) cellular respiration - the animals burn most of what they eat just to stay alive, move around, keep their cells running, and all of that leaves as heat that nothing can eat; (2) not everything at a level actually gets eaten, a lot of the phytoplankton and zooplankton just die and get broken down by decomposers, so that energy goes sideways out of the chain; (3) of the food that does get eaten, not all of it gets digested and absorbed, so a chunk of it leaves as feces and other waste. Tuna calculation: tuna is a tertiary consumer, so there are three transfers between it and the phytoplankton. 50 kg tuna needs 50/0.10 = 500 kg of small fish, 500/0.10 = 5,000 kg of zooplankton, and 5,000/0.10 = 50,000 kg of phytoplankton. So about 50,000 kg.

Nitrogen starts as N2 gas in the air, which plants can't use because the triple bond is too strong. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (like Rhizobium in root nodules, and cyanobacteria in the water) fix N2 into ammonia, NH3, which picks up a proton in the soil and becomes ammonium, NH4+. Then nitrifying bacteria do nitrification in two steps: Nitrosomonas turns NH4+ into nitrite, NO2-, and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, NO3-. Nitrate is the form most plants take up through their roots. Inside the root the plant reduces the nitrate back down to NH4+ using nitrate reductase, and then the NH4+ gets attached to a carbon skeleton to build amino acids like glutamate. Those amino acids get moved up to the leaf and joined together by ribosomes into a protein.

Rainforests have the highest GPP because everything a photosynthesizing plant needs is at its maximum there at the same time. Light: they're at the equator so day length and sun angle barely change all year, so there's high intensity light 12 hours a day 365 days a year, while boreal forests get low-angle light and very short winter days. Temperature: it stays warm (around 25-27 C) all year, which is near the optimum for rubisco and the Calvin cycle enzymes, so photosynthesis basically never shuts down, while taiga is below freezing for months and the trees are dormant. Water: rainfall is high and year-round so stomata can stay open without the plant risking drying out, and boreal soils are frozen a lot of the year so water isn't even available to take up. Nutrient cycling: it's warm and wet so decomposers work extremely fast and nutrients get released and taken back up almost immediately, versus taiga where cold, acidic, waterlogged soil makes decomposition really slow and nutrients stay locked up in the litter. Total area doesn't matter for GPP because GPP is per square meter, not the whole biome added up.

r = b - d, so r = 0.28 - 0.11 = 0.17 per year. N(t) = N0 * e^(rt) N(3) = 980 * e^(0.17*3) = 980 * e^(0.51) e^(0.51) is about 1.665 = 980 * 1.665 = about 1,632 finches after 3 years. Exponential growth can't keep going forever because the exponential model assumes resources are unlimited and that nothing is holding the population back - no competition, no predators, no disease, unlimited seeds and nesting spots. That's not how a real island works. Daphne Major is only about 0.34 km^2 and there is only so much seed on it. As N gets bigger, each bird gets a smaller share of the seeds, so more birds starve and fewer of them can raise chicks. That means the per capita birth rate drops and/or the per capita death rate goes up, so r itself shrinks. Once r hits 0 the population stops growing, which is the carrying capacity. Basically the growth curve bends from a J shape into an S shape.

K is about 1,200 birds. The evidence is the last part of the table. From 1982 on the numbers are 1,180, 1,210, 1,195, 1,200, 1,205. That's eight years where the population isn't trending up or down anymore, it's just wobbling in a narrow band right around 1,200. Before that (1978-1982) the population was climbing fast, 380 to 820 to 1,180, and then it just stops climbing. A population that levels off and oscillates a little around one value is sitting at its carrying capacity, because the island can't support more than that. As the population gets close to K the growth rate slows down. In the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, the (K-N)/K part is the thing that matters. When N is small, (K-N)/K is close to 1 so the population grows almost exponentially. When N gets near 1,200, K-N gets close to 0, so the whole term goes to about 0 and dN/dt goes to about 0 too. The fastest growth is at N = K/2, which here is about 600 birds, and looking at the table that's around 1972-1974 when the population jumped 480 to 750. So growth rate is highest in the middle and then falls off to nothing at K.

The 1977 drought is DENSITY-INDEPENDENT. Justification: the drought is a climate thing, it doesn't care how many finches are on the island. If there had been 100 finches or 10,000 finches, the rain still doesn't fall and the plants still don't make seeds, and roughly the same fraction of the birds die either way. The severity of the effect isn't set by the density of the population, it's set by an abiotic factor, so it's density-independent. (i) Food competition as density-dependent: Daphne Major produces a roughly fixed amount of seed in a normal year. When there are only 300 birds, each bird can find plenty of seeds, especially the easy small ones. As the population climbs toward 1,200, that same seed supply gets split more ways, so per capita food goes down. Birds then have to eat the big tough seeds they're bad at cracking, more of them starve, and females that are underweight lay fewer eggs. So the death rate rises and the birth rate falls specifically BECAUSE density went up - the strength of the effect depends on N, which is what density-dependent means. (ii) Disease transmission as density-dependent: when the population is dense the birds are packed closer together, feeding at the same seed patches and roosting near each other. A pathogen needs contact between an infected bird and a susceptible bird to spread, and the rate of those contacts goes up as density goes up (transmission is proportional to infected density times susceptible density). At low density an infected bird might die without ever passing it on, but at 1,200 birds on a tiny island an outbreak can rip through the whole flock. So a bigger proportion of the population gets sick and dies at high density than at low density, which limits the population more as it grows.

Hypothesis: If food availability rather than predation is the primary factor setting K for G. fortis, then adding extra seed will raise the population a plot can hold, while removing hawks and owls will not. Independent variable: what I manipulate - the amount of food available, and separately whether predators can get in. Dependent variable: the finch population size each plot levels off at (the K it reaches), counted by mark-recapture censuses twice a year for 5 years. Control group: fenced-off study plots on Daphne Major (or a nearby island with the same habitat) that are left completely alone - natural seed only, hawks and owls have normal access. Experimental groups: Group 1 - food supplement. I put out measured seed trays (same mix of small and large seeds) every week, predators left alone. Group 2 - predator exclusion. Netting/wire over the plot that keeps hawks and short-eared owls out but lets finches move, food left natural. Group 3 - both, food added AND predators excluded, to see if they interact. I'd use at least 4 replicate plots per treatment, all the same area, and assign which plot gets which treatment randomly. Prediction: if food is the primary limit, Group 1 and Group 3 settle at a higher population than control, and Group 2 looks about the same as control. If predation is the primary limit, it's the other way around, Group 2 goes up and Group 1 doesn't. Confounding variable: seasonal variation in seed production. Daphne Major has wet years and dry years and the seed crop swings a lot between them, so a plot could look like it has a higher K just because it got measured in a good rain year, not because of my treatment. To control for that I would run the experiment for five straight years so every plot experiences several wet and dry seasons, and then average each plot's population across all of those seasons so the year to year swings cancel out. Another thing that could mess it up is birds flying between plots, since Daphne Major is small enough that finches could just move to whichever plot has free seed and inflate that count. I'd control that by color-banding every bird so I know which plot it belongs to and can throw out or account for the immigrants when I calculate each plot's population.

Nitrogen starts as N2 gas in the air, which plants can't use because the triple bond is too strong. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (like Rhizobium in root nodules, and cyanobacteria in the water) fix N2 into ammonia, NH3, which picks up a proton in the soil and becomes ammonium, NH4+. Then nitrifying bacteria do nitrification in two steps: Nitrosomonas turns NH4+ into nitrite, NO2-, and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, NO3-. Nitrate is the form most plants take up through their roots. Inside the root the plant reduces the nitrate back down to NH4+ using nitrate reductase, and then the NH4+ gets attached to a carbon skeleton to build amino acids like glutamate. Exponential growth can't keep going forever because the exponential model assumes resources are unlimited and that nothing is holding the population back - no competition, no predators, no disease, unlimited seeds and nesting spots. That's not how a real island works. Daphne Major is only about 0.34 km^2 and there is only so much seed on it. As N gets bigger, each bird gets a smaller share of the seeds, so more birds starve and fewer of them can raise chicks. That means the per capita birth rate drops and/or the per capita death rate goes up, so r itself shrinks. Once r hits 0 the population stops growing, which is the carrying capacity. Basically the growth curve bends from a J shape into an S shape.

K is about 1,200 birds. The evidence is the last part of the table. From 1982 on the numbers are 1,180, 1,210, 1,195, 1,200, 1,205. That's eight years where the population isn't trending up or down anymore, it's just wobbling in a narrow band right around 1,200. Before that (1978-1982) the population was climbing fast, 380 to 820 to 1,180, and then it just stops climbing. A population that levels off and oscillates a little around one value is sitting at its carrying capacity, because the island can't support more than that. As the population gets close to K the growth rate slows down. In the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, the (K-N)/K part is the thing that matters. When N is small, (K-N)/K is close to 1 so the population grows almost exponentially. When N gets near 1,200, K-N gets close to 0, so the whole term goes to about 0 and dN/dt goes to about 0 too. The fastest growth is at N = K/2, which here is about 600 birds, and looking at the table that's around 1972-1974 when the population jumped 480 to 750. So growth rate is highest in the middle and then falls off to nothing at K. Notice the growth rate slowing doesn't mean the population is shrinking, it just means it's adding fewer birds each year.

The 1977 drought is DENSITY-INDEPENDENT. Justification: the drought is a climate thing, it doesn't care how many finches are on the island. If there had been 100 finches or 10,000 finches, the rain still doesn't fall and the plants still don't make seeds, and roughly the same fraction of the birds die either way. The severity of the effect isn't set by the density of the population, it's set by an abiotic factor, so it's density-independent. (i) Food competition as density-dependent: Daphne Major produces a roughly fixed amount of seed in a normal year. When there are only 300 birds, each bird can find plenty of seeds, especially the easy small ones. As the population climbs toward 1,200, that same seed supply gets split more ways, so per capita food goes down. Birds then have to eat the big tough seeds they're bad at cracking, more of them starve, and females that are underweight lay fewer eggs. So the death rate rises and the birth rate falls specifically BECAUSE density went up - the strength of the effect depends on N, which is what density-dependent means. (ii) Disease transmission as density-dependent: when the population is dense the birds are packed closer together, feeding at the same seed patches and roosting near each other. A pathogen needs contact between an infected bird and a susceptible bird to spread, and the rate of those contacts goes up as density goes up (transmission is proportional to infected density times susceptible density). At low density an infected bird might die without ever passing it on, but at 1,200 birds on a tiny island an outbreak can rip through the whole flock. So a bigger proportion of the population gets sick and dies at high density than at low density, which limits the population more as it grows.

Hypothesis: If food availability rather than predation is the primary factor setting K for G. fortis, then adding extra seed will raise the population a plot can hold, while removing hawks and owls will not. Independent variable: what I manipulate - the amount of food available, and separately whether predators can get in. Dependent variable: the finch population size each plot levels off at (the K it reaches), counted by mark-recapture censuses twice a year for 5 years. Control group: fenced-off study plots on Daphne Major (or a nearby island with the same habitat) that are left completely alone - natural seed only, hawks and owls have normal access. Experimental groups: Group 1 - food supplement. I put out measured seed trays (same mix of small and large seeds) every week, predators left alone. Group 2 - predator exclusion. Netting/wire over the plot that keeps hawks and short-eared owls out but lets finches move, food left natural. Group 3 - both, food added AND predators excluded, to see if they interact. I'd use at least 4 replicate plots per treatment, all the same area, and assign which plot gets which treatment randomly. Prediction: if food is the primary limit, Group 1 and Group 3 settle at a higher population than control, and Group 2 looks about the same as control. If predation is the primary limit, it's the other way around, Group 2 goes up and Group 1 doesn't. Confounding variable: seasonal variation in seed production. Daphne Major has wet years and dry years and the seed crop swings a lot between them, so a plot could look like it has a higher K just because it got measured in a good rain year, not because of my treatment. To control for that I would run the experiment for five straight years so every plot experiences several wet and dry seasons, and then average each plot's population across all of those seasons so the year to year swings cancel out. Another thing that could mess it up is birds flying between plots, since Daphne Major is small enough that finches could just move to whichever plot has free seed and inflate that count. Why exponential growth can't go on forever: the exponential model is built on the assumption that nothing is limiting - infinite seeds, infinite nest sites, no predators, no disease, and every bird reproduces at the same rate no matter how crowded it is. In the real world Daphne Major is a tiny island with a fixed seed supply. As N goes up, resources per bird go down, birds compete, and the ones that lose the competition starve or fail to breed. That pushes the per capita death rate up and the per capita birth rate down, so r shrinks over time instead of staying at 0.17. Eventually births equal deaths and the population flattens out at the carrying capacity. If it didn't, you'd have millions of finches on a 0.34 km^2 rock, which obviously can't happen.

Carrying capacity K = about 1,200 birds. Evidence: after the population recovers from the drought it climbs to 1,180 in 1982 and then basically stops. 1984 is 1,210, 1986 is 1,195, 1988 is 1,200, 1990 is 1,205. Those are all within about 30 birds of each other over 8 years with no trend either direction, just small oscillation. That flat plateau is the signature of a population sitting at K - the island can support around 1,200 finches and no more. The fact that it slightly overshoots to 1,210 and then dips back to 1,195 is normal overshoot/undershoot around K. What happens to growth rate as N approaches K: the growth rate keeps dropping. From 1978 to 1980 the population added 440 birds in two years, from 1980 to 1982 it added 360, and from 1982 to 1984 it only added 30. So each year the population is adding fewer and fewer individuals until it's adding basically zero. In logistic terms dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K and (K-N)/K shrinks toward zero as N approaches K, so dN/dt goes to zero.

The 1977 drought = DENSITY-INDEPENDENT limiting factor. Why: whether the drought kills a given bird has nothing to do with how many other birds are on the island. Rainfall is abiotic. A drought that wipes out the seed crop would have knocked out roughly the same percentage of the finches if the population had been 200 or 2,000. The trigger is climate, not crowding, so the effect isn't a function of density. Density-dependent factors get stronger as N rises; the drought would've hit just as hard at low N. (i) Food competition, density-dependent: the seed supply on Daphne Major is basically fixed per year. Divide that fixed supply by more and more birds and each individual gets less. At 300 birds there's plenty of the small easy seeds to go around; at 1,200 birds the small seeds get stripped fast and a lot of finches are stuck trying to crack big Tribulus seeds that only the biggest-beaked birds can handle. So starvation goes up and reproductive success goes down, and how bad it gets scales directly with how many birds there are - that's the definition of density-dependent. (ii) Disease transmission, density-dependent: pathogens spread by contact, so the more crowded the birds are the more contacts happen per bird per day. At high density they're packed onto the same seed patches and roosts, so an infected finch passes it to many others before it dies, and the disease can take off. At low density the same pathogen may burn out because the sick bird never runs into enough susceptible birds. So the fraction of the population killed by disease rises as density rises, which pushes the death rate up right when the population is largest.

Hypothesis: If food availability (not predation) is what sets the carrying capacity of G. fortis on Daphne Major, then plots given extra seed will support a larger stable population than untreated plots, while plots with hawks and owls excluded will not differ from untreated plots. Independent variable: seed availability (natural vs supplemented) and predator access (open vs excluded). Dependent variable: the stable population size each plot settles at, measured by banding every bird and doing mark-recapture counts every 6 months. Control group: plots left totally unmanipulated - natural seed crop, hawks and short-eared owls able to hunt normally. Experimental groups: Group 1: seed added on a fixed weekly schedule, predators have normal access. Group 2: predator exclusion netting over the plot, seed left at natural levels. Group 3: seed added AND predators excluded.
